title: The Gang Spies Like U.S.

jokes.text: That's what's good about a beer. It's good. It just keeps cycling through you.
jokes.setup: Two guys drinking beer, seemingly about to say something profound about it
jokes.punchline: The 'profound' observation is that beer keeps cycling through you — i.e., you urinate it out
jokes.explanation: Classic Always Sunny cold open — Charlie and Frank delivering a dumb observation with total sincerity. Works on character but the joke itself is mild. Functional opener.

dialogue.line: We got news, we've got terrible news.

jokes.text: So many omegas... threes, fours and fives.
jokes.setup: Gang discussing the health benefits of fish, mentioning omega-3 fatty acids
jokes.punchline: Charlie lists 'threes, fours and fives' as if omega-4 and omega-5 are real things, delivered with total confidence
jokes.explanation: Perfect Charlie moment — he half-knows something real (omega-3s) and confidently extends it into nonsense. The character integration is excellent; this joke only works coming from Charlie. Good economy.

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: That's what's good about a beer.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: Yeah. It just keeps cycling through...

jokes.text: Melts in your mouth. You get to eat all your scales.
jokes.setup: Gang rhapsodizing about delicious fish
jokes.punchline: Charlie adds that you 'get to eat all your scales' as a selling point, implying he eats fish scales as a delicacy
jokes.explanation: Charlie's feral dietary habits are a reliable vein of humor in the show. 'You get to eat all your scales' is delivered as a genuine perk, which is perfectly wrong in a Charlie-specific way. The escalation from normal fish appreciation into scale-eating is well-structured.

dialogue.line: Protein, omega numbers... Omega threes, fours and fives.

jokes.text: Don't eat the scales. / You won't get scales unless it's a fish or a reptile. / Don't eat reptiles. / I'm not eating all reptiles, just the good ones.
jokes.setup: Gang corrects Charlie about eating scales; the correction attempt spirals
jokes.punchline: Charlie concedes he won't eat ALL reptiles, just 'the good ones' — implying he has a curated list of edible reptiles
jokes.explanation: This is a tight escalating sequence that builds beautifully. Each beat adds a new layer of absurdity and the final 'just the good ones' perfectly caps it. The structure is clean — setup, complication, false resolution, true punchline. Charlie's reptile diet being a discerning one is a great character detail. Strong writing.

dialogue.line: You get to eat all your scales.

jokes.text: Don't eat reptiles and... just hang out.
jokes.setup: Mac and Dennis are dismissing Frank and Charlie from the spy mission
jokes.punchline: Dennis summarizes their instructions as 'don't eat reptiles' — a callback to the previous absurd conversation — as if that's a standing instruction needed for Charlie
jokes.explanation: A quick callback that earns its laugh through brevity. The fact that Dennis treats 'don't eat reptiles' as a legitimate standing order for Charlie is a great character beat. Well-executed economy.

dialogue.line: Yeah, not eating all reptiles, just the good ones.

jokes.text: Is this 'cause you guys have been living at her place ever since your fire?
jokes.setup: Mac and Dennis choosing Dee over Frank and Charlie for the spy mission
jokes.punchline: Frank points out the real reason — Mac and Dennis burned down their apartment and have been living with Dee, creating a forced alliance
jokes.explanation: Functional exposition delivered as a comedic reveal. The situation (mac and dennis burned their own place down) is funnier than this particular line, which is essentially setup for the larger Dee dynamic. Gets the job done.

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: You're gonna help us gather intel.

dialogue.speaker: Dee
dialogue.line: Really? Let's do it, come on.

jokes.text: Let's... Let's not get crazy, Dee. You're always gonna be the butt of our jokes. Whatever. Let's roll.
jokes.setup: Dee argues she shouldn't be the butt of everyone's jokes anymore since Mac and Dennis living with her proved she's cool
jokes.punchline: Dennis flatly states 'You're always gonna be the butt of our jokes' as a matter of settled fact, then immediately moves on
jokes.explanation: Dennis's casual cruelty delivered with zero malice is quintessential Always Sunny. The 'let's not get crazy' preface, followed by the blunt declaration, then the immediate pivot to 'let's roll' captures the gang's dynamic perfectly. Highly quotable. Dennis-specific character work.

dialogue.line: You're completely unreliable, Dee, really. You're, like, all gangly and uncoordinated.

jokes.text: Something stinks here, Charlie, and it ain't just the fish.
jokes.setup: Frank suspects Mac and Dennis are hiding something; the Chinese fish factory across the street literally stinks
jokes.punchline: Frank delivers the classic 'something stinks and it ain't the [obvious smell]' construction with total sincerity
jokes.explanation: This is a clichéd construction ('something stinks and it ain't X') that gets a mild chuckle from the fish context. Too lazy a construction for Always Sunny, which usually subverts these tropes rather than playing them straight. Below average for the show.

dialogue.speaker: Frank
dialogue.line: Something stinks here, Charlie, and it ain't just the fish.

jokes.text: Well, you know the Chinese. It's business first, breathing second.
jokes.setup: Gang enters the fish factory and the air quality is terrible
jokes.punchline: Mac offers a casually racist 'explanation' for the poor working conditions with the confidence of someone who thinks they're being insightful
jokes.explanation: Classic Always Sunny approach: the joke is that Mac is casually, obliviously racist, not that the observation is correct. The 'business first, breathing second' construction is economical and captures the character well. Mid-tier execution.

dialogue.speaker: Frank
dialogue.line: Charlie, I trust the Chinese as far as I could throw their factory.

jokes.text: Human rights violations, anything, Dee. Just-Just, you know, gather intel.
jokes.setup: Mac and Dennis briefing Dee on what to look for in the fish factory
jokes.punchline: The list of things to look for escalates to 'human rights violations' tossed in casually as just another line item, then immediately dismissed with 'anything, Dee'
jokes.explanation: The casualness with which Mac and Dennis treat 'human rights violations' as a minor intel concern is a solid dark joke. The 'anything, Dee' dismissal lands well. Competent but not exceptional.

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: Well, you know the Chinese. It's like, business first, breathing second, goddamn it!

jokes.text: Dee, you're on a need-to-know basis here. There's a chain of command here. You're at the very bottom. You're way down.
jokes.setup: Dee reasonably asks what the whole plan is
jokes.punchline: Mac invokes an elaborate chain-of-command structure to justify keeping Dee in the dark, despite the 'operation' being two guys walking into a fish factory
jokes.explanation: Mac's delusion about being a military-style operator is a consistent character note. 'You're way down' as a secondary confirmation is a good beat. Solid but familiar territory for Mac.

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: He'll love how 'pretty' and 'blonde' you are.

jokes.text: He'll love how 'pretty' and 'blonde' you are. / Don't do that. I'm blonde.
jokes.setup: Mac tells Dee to flirt with the manager and he'll love how pretty and blonde she is — with audible air quotes around 'pretty'
jokes.punchline: Dennis then says 'Don't do that. I'm blonde' — objecting only to the air-quoting of 'blonde', not 'pretty', revealing his vanity and missing the insult to Dee entirely
jokes.explanation: This is a gem of character-based comedy. Mac air-quotes 'pretty' (implying Dee isn't) but not 'blonde,' and Dennis's narcissistic objection is ONLY to the slight against blondes — because he's blonde. The layered joke (insult to Dee, Dennis's vanity, the implicit team-up against Dee, Dennis not defending her at all) is efficiently delivered. Strong character integration.

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: I wanted to apologize about, um, snapping earlier today with words at you guys, and then I came here to make an apology... apology words.

jokes.text: It sucks not having our own apartment. We got to get back in there. I know. I hate Dee. Dennis, I hate her.
jokes.setup: Mac and Dennis are living with Dee after burning their own place down — having just recruited her for a mission
jokes.punchline: The moment she's gone, Mac declares he hates Dee with sincere desperation: 'Dennis, I hate her.' — the name-usage amplifying the genuine feeling
jokes.explanation: The pivot from using Dee to immediate loathing is a good gang dynamic beat. 'Dennis, I hate her' has a nice desperate quality. The hypocrisy is a consistent Always Sunny engine. Solid mid-tier joke.

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: S... spider crawled up in my ear. It was living there. Right. Sends its thoughts to me.

jokes.text: I know, but at least we got her out of our hair for a little while... and we can finally do our plan.
jokes.setup: Mac and Dennis conspiring; they refer to their secret 'plan' that they needed privacy for
jokes.punchline: The ominous secrecy and anti-Dee scheming is set up to suggest something nefarious — but will be revealed as simply watching porn / researching cream pies
jokes.explanation: This functions primarily as a misdirection setup — scoring higher on rewatch when the reveal is known. On first watch, it's mysterious; it pays off much later. The rewatch bonus is merited but the joke in isolation is mild.

dialogue.line: Who's Roger?

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: Just... thinking about legally changing my name to Roger.

jokes.text: I wanted to apologize about, um, snapping earlier today... with words at you guys, and then I came here to make an apology... apology words.
jokes.setup: Charlie shows up at Mac and Dennis's door to apologize
jokes.punchline: His apology devolves into recursive verbal confusion: 'apology... apology words' — he can't complete a sentence, treating 'words' as a noun he needs to supply separately
jokes.explanation: Charlie's illiteracy and broken verbal processing is a show staple, but 'apology words' as a complete thought is a particularly good example of it. The redundancy of 'apology... apology words' captures his fumbling perfectly. Strong character integration.

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: Spider, can I leave?

dialogue.speaker: Spider
dialogue.line: To the left.

jokes.text: What's he talking about? I don't know. I don't remember. Okay, thank you.
jokes.setup: Charlie shows up claiming to apologize for 'snapping' at them earlier with words
jokes.punchline: Mac and Dennis have zero memory of whatever Charlie is referring to and simply want him gone, so they accept the apology they don't understand
jokes.explanation: Good reaction beat — the gang's social indifference (accepting an apology for something they can't even recall) is funny, but it's a brief beat serving the spy-flowers scene more than landing as a standalone joke.

dialogue.speaker: Fish Factory Worker
dialogue.line: No. I didn't get that. You chop fish, pull gut!

jokes.text: You can't just have it. There's a plan. I have to come in and give it to you. And put it down.
jokes.setup: Charlie has brought Mac and Dennis a flower arrangement as a pretext to plant a spy device; Mac and Dennis just want him gone
jokes.punchline: Charlie insists there is a protocol — he must physically enter and place the flowers — announced in a hushed, procedural tone as if running a covert op
jokes.explanation: The gap between Charlie's elaborate spy logic and the mundane reality of 'just put the flowers down' is well-played. His procedural narration of his own movements ('I have to come in and give it to you. And put it down.') is delightfully unhinged. Rewatch value since you know the bug is in the vase.

dialogue.speaker: Dee
dialogue.line: It got me! It got me good! Aah! It got in my mouth!

jokes.text: No, to the left. / To the left, you say? / Didn't say that. / Don't talk out loud to me. / Roger that. / Who's Roger?
jokes.setup: Frank is guiding Charlie via earpiece to position the bugged vase; Mac and Dennis are right there
jokes.punchline: Charlie responds to Frank's earpiece directions out loud, calling attention to himself; then 'Roger that' triggers Mac/Dennis to genuinely ask 'Who's Roger?' — they don't know the radio term
jokes.explanation: The 'Roger that / Who's Roger?' beat is a genuinely good joke — the gangsters' ignorance of a basic radio term executed with sincere confusion. Combined with Charlie speaking out loud while supposedly being covert, the scene builds comedic tension well. The structure of the exchange is tight and each beat escalates the absurdity.

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: I'm to remember every man I've seen fall into a plate of spaghetti?

jokes.text: Just... Thinking about legally changing my name to Roger.
jokes.setup: Mac and Dennis ask 'Who's Roger?' after Charlie says 'Roger that' into his earpiece
jokes.punchline: Charlie covers by claiming he's thinking of legally changing his name to Roger — a completely unrelated and unprovable non-explanation
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best jokes. Charlie's improvised cover story is so absurd yet so specifically Charlie that it becomes perfect. The economy is exceptional — one sentence that tells you everything about how Charlie's brain works under pressure. 'Thinking about legally changing my name to Roger' as a deflection is the kind of non-sequitur that only Charlie could produce, and it somehow almost works because it's so weird. Highly quotable, strong rewatch value.

dialogue.speaker: Dee
dialogue.line: Uh, hell no, lady, no. Uh, look, I realize this might all be moon talk to you, but I'm not touching fish guts with my hands, okay?

jokes.text: What's wrong with your ear, dude? / Just... A spider crawled up in my ear. It's living there. / Right. / Sends its thoughts to me.
jokes.setup: Mac and Dennis notice Charlie has an earpiece and ask what's wrong with his ear
jokes.punchline: Charlie explains there's a spider living in his ear that sends its thoughts to him — presented as a viable alternative explanation, and Dennis simply accepts it with 'Right'
jokes.explanation: This is the episode's best joke. The spider explanation is brilliantly calibrated — it's crazy enough that it obviously isn't true, but Dennis's flat 'Right' acceptance is funnier because (a) Dennis apparently finds this more plausible than a hidden earpiece, (b) it perfectly characterizes how the gang just rolls with Charlie's insanity, and (c) 'Sends its thoughts to me' as a follow-up after a beat is timed perfectly. The character integration is near-perfect — this could only be Charlie, and Dennis's acceptance could only be Dennis. Highly quotable and would absolutely get a big laugh from a group audience.

dialogue.speaker: Dee
dialogue.line: Just send it all over the place! Nobody will know.

jokes.text: Is it telling you to leave?
jokes.setup: Charlie has explained a spider lives in his ear and sends its thoughts
jokes.punchline: Dennis, within the logic of this insane claim, asks if the spider is telling Charlie to leave — turning the absurdity into a practical request
jokes.explanation: Dennis's total commitment to the spider's authority — engaging with its fictional agency to get Charlie to leave — is a perfect deadpan beat. It doubles as a callback and an escalation. The economy is flawless: five words that build on the previous joke and get a second laugh from the same premise. Dennis operating within absurd logic without breaking is classic.

dialogue.speaker: Frank
dialogue.line: You're talking to me like you know me. Have we ever met?

jokes.text: Hey, man. Can you hear and see everything? / They're talking about research. Research, huh?
jokes.setup: Mac and Dennis are excitedly discussing their secret 'research' while Charlie listens through the hidden bug
jokes.punchline: Charlie relays this to Frank with barely-informed surveillance commentary: 'They're talking about research. Research, huh?' — as if 'research' is damning intel
jokes.explanation: Charlie treating the word 'research' as suspicious intel is a good character beat. The conspiratorial 'Research, huh?' delivery mirrors how spy movies treat benign information as ominous. Mid-tier but functional.

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: Asians... and cream pies.

jokes.text: So what's the deal with these masks, huh? Are they gonna protect you from the fish or protect the fish from you? Am I right?
jokes.setup: Dee has gotten a job at the fish factory and is trying to ingratiate herself with coworkers by doing stand-up-style observations
jokes.punchline: The joke is terrible ('protect the fish from you'), delivered to workers who don't respond or understand her — and the 'am I right?' hanging in silence
jokes.explanation: The joke is intentionally bad — it's Dee's failed attempt at workplace humor. The comedy is in the cringe of her trying and failing, not in the content of the joke itself. The 'am I right?' with no response is the actual punchline. Solid cringe beat but familiar territory for the show.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: Why do you look familiar to me?

dialogue.speaker: Waiter
dialogue.line: I'm the waiter you didn't tip earlier.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: Yeah, well, you're not gonna get tipped again with that attitude.

jokes.text: No. I didn't get that. / You chop fish, pull gut!
jokes.setup: Dee has just delivered her mask joke to a factory worker
jokes.punchline: The worker's response is simply a command to do her job: 'You chop fish, pull gut!' — a total dismissal of her attempted bonding
jokes.explanation: 'Chop fish, pull gut' is a satisfyingly blunt dismissal that also becomes a running refrain. The worker's total indifference to Dee's social overtures perfectly deflates her. Good economy.

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: I like cream pies as much as the next guy.

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: Oh, shh... don't-don't say it out loud.

jokes.text: Hi. Um... Uh, my name's Dee, and I'm new around here, and I just would love to chat with you sometime in private, you know? Maybe up in your secret private office up there?
jokes.setup: Dee has been told to flirt with the manager and get access to his office
jokes.punchline: Dee's flirting is so bad that she immediately announces she wants access to his 'secret private office' — combining clumsy seduction with obvious surveillance intent
jokes.explanation: Dee's incompetence at the simplest possible task (flirting to gain access) is well-characterized. The 'secret private office' line inadvertently reveals her actual motive in the most transparent way. Solid Dee moment.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: I do not want to taste your cream pie.

jokes.text: American girl, blue eyes, blonde hair... Aaah! / It's got me! It's got me good! Aaah! / It's in my mouth. It's getting in...
jokes.setup: Dee is trying to charm the manager by pointing out her assets — 'American girl, blue eyes, blonde hair'
jokes.punchline: Mid-pitch, a fish apparently flops up and attacks/covers her face, cutting off her seduction attempt completely
jokes.explanation: Physical comedy at Dee's expense — cutting off her self-promotion mid-sentence with a fish attack is appropriately absurd. 'It's got me good!' has a good desperate quality. Visual comedy that works within Always Sunny's Dee-humiliation tradition. The 'It's in my mouth' escalation earns its laugh.

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: I'd love watching a kid do it.

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: Dude, you are gonna get in a lot of trouble.

jokes.text: Oh, yeah. Uh, well, our friendship's in danger, so... I stole Frank's credit card. You guys want to have lunch?
jokes.setup: Mac and Dennis rush over after Charlie texts them 911 — an emergency
jokes.punchline: The 'friendship emergency' is Charlie wanting to have lunch, funded by Frank's stolen credit card — the 911 was not a real emergency and his logic is characteristically warped
jokes.explanation: Classic Charlie move — 'our friendship's in danger' as the preamble to stealing a credit card for lunch. The logic is impeccably Charlie: friendship is at stake, so I committed theft, so let's eat. Well-structured misdirection with strong character integration.

dialogue.line: What kind of cream pie are you talking about? What... kind of cream pie are you talking about?

jokes.text: I'm annoyed, but I could eat.
jokes.setup: Mac learns Charlie stole Frank's credit card just to get them to come to lunch
jokes.punchline: Mac's objection is immediately overridden by his desire to eat, compressed into one perfectly calibrated line
jokes.explanation: Perfect economy — five words that capture Mac's entire moral framework. He has a minor ethical objection that is instantly defeated by appetite. Highly quotable, applicable beyond the show. The best kind of simple line.

dialogue.speaker: Narrator
dialogue.line: Cream pies are a rich American tradition and also delicious.

jokes.text: I'm sorry. Do I know you, pal? I've never seen this man before in my life. / I waited on you before. You tied my shoelaces together. I fell down. / I'm getting nothing. I'm drawing a blank on this guy.
jokes.setup: The gang returns to Guigino's restaurant where the waiter recognizes them from a previous incident
jokes.punchline: Dennis claims total amnesia about a man whose shoelaces he tied together, causing him to fall into scalding spaghetti — delivered with zero guilt or recognition
jokes.explanation: Dennis's total blankness about a victim he personally harmed is perfectly in character — his narcissism means other people simply don't register. 'A scalding hot plate of spaghetti fell into my face' vs. 'I'm to remember every man I've seen fall into a plate of spaghetti?' is a great exchange. The implied history is funnier than what's shown. This sets up the callback payoff later.

dialogue.speaker: Frank
dialogue.line: Holy shit! Holy shit...

jokes.text: No, I'm in a fish mood now. Fish has been established. / It was established, wasn't it? / Yeah, it was. So three snappers. / Why are we talking about it so much? Get the goddamn snappers.
jokes.setup: The snapper is $44; they should get something cheaper
jokes.punchline: Mac declares fish 'established' as a category, the group validates this as if it's legally binding, and then Dennis complains about the very conversation he prolonged
jokes.explanation: The gang's group logic about fish being 'established' and then immediately Meta-complaining about the conversation they're having is a good piece of absurdist gang behavior. 'Fish has been established' has quotable potential. Escalates satisfyingly.

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: We're out of snapper, Dee!

jokes.text: Actually, our fish supplier had an incident at their facility, so we are limited on fish. Market price is quite high today.
jokes.setup: Dennis orders the snapper; this is the first appearance of the fish shortage plot payoff
jokes.punchline: The restaurant's fish supply has been disrupted — unknown to the gang, this is because Dee shut down the Chinese factory with her accidents
jokes.explanation: More of a structural plant than a joke in itself — it only fully pays off at the end of the episode when we learn Dee caused it. Gets a rewatch bonus because on second viewing you appreciate the construction, but on first viewing it's setup.

dialogue.speaker: Frank
dialogue.line: I think what you're gonna find when you're spying on the general population is that everyone is just, uh... masturbating, constantly. I know I am.

jokes.text: Ha. Charlie, I'm in.
jokes.setup: Frank has somehow gotten himself into the Chinese fish factory while Charlie keeps Mac and Dennis at lunch
jokes.punchline: Frank's confident, brief check-in — 'I'm in' — implying he's executed a covert infiltration, contrasted with what is presumably Frank bumbling around a fish factory
jokes.explanation: Brief scene transition beat — Frank's spy confidence is a mild joke. Functions as a scene connector more than a standalone comedic moment. Mid-low tier.

jokes.text: Damn it. Sweeping up fish guts with a broom? Got to be some kind of workers' rights violation. / What are you... Aaah, you idiot! Are you picking it up with your hands?
jokes.setup: Dee is tasked with sweeping fish guts and objects to the method
jokes.punchline: The supervisor screams at her because she's picking up fish guts with her bare hands instead of using the broom she was complaining about
jokes.explanation: Dee's self-defeating logic — complaining about the method, then doing something worse — is a good character beat. The supervisor's exasperation is well-timed. Solid cringe-physical hybrid.

jokes.text: Look, I realize this might all be moon talk to you, but I'm not touching fish guts with my hands, okay? / You know what we could do? Yeah, like just disperse it. You know what I mean? Just send it all over the place. Nobody will know. Just kind of... There we go.
jokes.setup: Dee refuses to handle fish guts and proposes an alternative method
jokes.punchline: Her 'alternative' is to disperse/scatter the fish guts everywhere so they're less visible — which is obviously worse. 'Nobody will know' and 'There we go' as self-satisfaction make it.
jokes.explanation: Dee's problem-solving failure is characteristically self-serving and stupid. 'Moon talk' as a phrase she uses casually is a good detail. The satisfied 'There we go' while scattering fish guts is a good character moment.

jokes.text: Hi, Frank. Sweet hat and jacket. / Don't... Charlie, don't sit there. / Huh? / Sit back there. We gotta be smart about this.
jokes.setup: Frank and Charlie meeting at the restaurant where they're supposed to be spying on Mac and Dennis
jokes.punchline: Frank is at the restaurant too — their cover is immediately useless — but he insists they 'be smart about this' by sitting at different tables in the same visible restaurant
jokes.explanation: Classic Always Sunny incompetent spy work — Frank and Charlie's 'covert' operation is just sitting in the same restaurant. 'Sweet hat and jacket' as the greeting from Charlie before Frank shushes him is a nice detail. Functional but not among the episode's stronger moments.

jokes.text: Gentlemen, I hate to inform you two... strangers here, that we are out of snapper.
jokes.setup: Frank and Charlie are pretending not to know Mac and Dennis; the waiter has to deliver bad news to both tables simultaneously
jokes.punchline: The waiter's stressed pause before 'strangers here' — playing along with their absurd cover while clearly irritated — is the joke
jokes.explanation: The waiter being forced to participate in their transparent cover story by calling them 'strangers' is a good running gag beat. The fish shortage callback connecting to Dee's factory destruction is a solid structural payoff.

jokes.text: You know what, Dennis? I'll have a plate of piping-hot spaghetti instead. Extra sauce.
jokes.setup: No fish available; Mac is forced to order something else. Earlier, the waiter mentioned falling into scalding spaghetti
jokes.punchline: Mac deliberately orders spaghetti 'extra sauce' — signaling intent to repeat the shoelace-spaghetti incident on the waiter
jokes.explanation: A beautifully constructed callback. Mac ordering 'piping-hot spaghetti, extra sauce' is immediately recognizable as a threat disguised as a food order, and the waiter's visible reaction must be devastating. 'Extra sauce' as the kicker is perfectly economical and signals premeditation. Dark humor at its best — the audience gets the joke before the characters explain it. Strong structure and character work.

jokes.text: So you do remember me.
jokes.setup: Mac and Dennis said they didn't remember the waiter; now Mac has ordered the specific spaghetti that burned him
jokes.punchline: The waiter's flat, resigned 'So you do remember me' is the perfect response to the implied threat
jokes.explanation: Four words that land perfectly. The waiter's weary recognition — delivered with zero surprise — that his tormentors have revealed themselves through their spaghetti order is a masterclass in economy. The callback structure is tight: they denied knowing him, then proved they did with the food order, and he calls it out with minimal words. Excellent.

jokes.text: I think Mac and Dennis are going into business with the Chinese guys across the street. / What? They're gonna open up some kind of pastry factory.
jokes.setup: Frank and Charlie piecing together Mac and Dennis's secret research from the laptop search history
jokes.punchline: The search terms 'Asians' and 'cream pies' lead Frank to conclude they're opening an Asian cream pie PASTRY factory — which is hilariously innocent given the alternative interpretation
jokes.explanation: The pivot on which the whole episode turns. The audience immediately understands 'Asians' + 'cream pies' in a browser history is pornography; Frank and Charlie reach the most innocent possible conclusion. The gap between what the audience knows and what the characters conclude is the engine of the entire second act. Well-structured dramatic irony with strong payoff potential.

jokes.text: They're gonna turn Paddy's into some kind of Asian cream pie factory! / Those bastards! / Sons of bitches! / Beat them at their own game. The Chinese want cream pies, they'll get cream pies. But only, they're not gonna get them from those bozos.
jokes.setup: Frank and Charlie have concluded Mac and Dennis are going into the cream pie pastry business with the Chinese factory
jokes.punchline: Their outrage is completely genuine and misdirected — they decide to compete in the cream pie business they've invented in their heads
jokes.explanation: The escalation of their misunderstanding into a business rivalry is satisfying. 'Those bastards!' for a crime that didn't happen in the way they think is a good beat. 'Beat them at their own game' applied to a pornographic search history misread as a bakery plan is the kind of layered misunderstanding Always Sunny does well.

jokes.text: Can I go now? / I feel like you had a really long session last time. / I did, yeah. I went on for a long time, but that's how much it takes. / I'm trying to build up to something, to a major finish.
jokes.setup: Mac and Dennis are discussing their secret 'research sessions' — the audience suspects but isn't yet sure they're watching pornography
jokes.punchline: 'A long session,' 'build up to something,' 'major finish' — all loaded double-entendre language that makes it increasingly clear they're discussing pornography while pretending it's about research
jokes.explanation: The deliberate obfuscation of what their 'research' is keeps the audience ahead of the other characters while maintaining plausible deniability in the dialogue. 'Build up to something, to a major finish' is transparently sexual but framed as professional. The cringe comes from Mac and Dennis's earnestness about whatever they're doing.

jokes.text: Classic. When he falls, it'll spill all over. / Yeah, the spaghetti will get on him. / I've always wanted to see that.
jokes.setup: Frank joins the table and they discuss tying the waiter's shoelaces together again
jokes.punchline: Frank says 'I've always wanted to see that' — implying he's envious of Mac and Dennis having done it before and wanting to witness the spaghetti shoelace trick firsthand
jokes.explanation: Frank's FOMO about the original spaghetti incident is a good dark beat. 'I've always wanted to see that' normalizes gang sadism as a shared entertainment. Good callback extension but slightly diminishing returns on the gag.

jokes.text: Listen, Frank's onto you. That's why I had Dee's Internet shut down. He knows what you're doing.
jokes.setup: Charlie has apparently taken independent espionage action to protect Mac and Dennis
jokes.punchline: Charlie casually reveals he sabotaged Dee's Internet (by which he means the factory WiFi) as a protective measure, without telling anyone — his freelance counter-intelligence is both touching and completely counterproductive
jokes.explanation: More of a plot mechanic than a pure joke, but Charlie's self-appointed loyalty mission has a funny quality. The implication that Charlie would just unilaterally cut off Internet access without telling anyone is very Charlie.

jokes.text: You don't have a goddamn cover. You're dressed like it's Halloween.
jokes.setup: Dee claims her 'cover is blown' at the restaurant and asks to sit with the gang
jokes.punchline: Mac points out she has no cover because she's dressed like it's Halloween — implying Dee's chosen disguise is a ridiculous costume
jokes.explanation: A good visual gag dependent on whatever absurd spy outfit Dee has chosen. The dismissal of her 'cover' via Halloween comparison is efficiently delivered. Dee's self-delusion about being covert is a good running element.

jokes.text: What? I'm not ashamed. / I'm a little bit ashamed, but I think that's natural.
jokes.setup: Charlie tells Mac and Dennis they should be ashamed of what they've been doing
jokes.punchline: Dennis's 'I'm a little bit ashamed, but I think that's natural' — expressing that mild shame about the activity is a normal response, suggesting awareness that it's shameful while continuing
jokes.explanation: Dennis's admission of natural shame is perfectly calibrated — it acknowledges wrongdoing while normalizing it in one breath. 'I think that's natural' about shame-worthy activity is a great character line. Mac's immediate denial vs. Dennis's nuanced shame is a good character contrast.

jokes.text: Now Frank wants to start doing it too. / So what? So what? Let him do it. / Well, he wants me to do it with him. / I assumed you two did that already. Me too.
jokes.setup: Charlie tells Mac and Dennis Frank wants to join their 'research sessions' — with 'it' referring to the cream pie business plan but sounding sexual
jokes.punchline: Mac and Dennis both assumed Frank and Charlie already 'did it' together — the double-meaning landing hard as the conversation sounds increasingly like it's about something sexual
jokes.explanation: The sustained double-entendre conversation is well-constructed — every line works on two levels simultaneously. 'I assumed you two did that already' spoken earnestly by Mac about Frank and Charlie is a great beat. The writing keeps both meanings alive without making either feel forced.

jokes.text: No! He wants us to do it with the Chinese guy across the street. / I knew you wouldn't be into that. / Well, no, I'm not into that. That's bizarre.
jokes.setup: Frank wants to partner with the Chinese factory for the cream pie business — but it sounds like he wants a sexual three-way with a stranger
jokes.punchline: Dennis says 'That's bizarre' about a business partnership that sounds like a sexual proposition involving the Chinese factory owner
jokes.explanation: The misunderstanding continues to build — now Frank wants to involve the Chinese factory owner, which in the sexual reading sounds like an escalating proposition. The double-meaning machine is running smoothly here.

jokes.text: I feel like I should be doing it with you guys. / Oh. / Come on, man. This is getting weird and messy. I don't want to get you involved. There's too many people.
jokes.setup: Charlie argues he should be part of Mac and Dennis's cream pie venture instead of doing it with Frank
jokes.punchline: Dennis says 'This is getting weird and messy. There's too many people' — which in the sexual reading is about a group activity, and in the business reading is about an overcrowded partnership
jokes.explanation: Continuing the double entendre chain. 'Weird and messy / too many people' works as sexual and business commentary simultaneously. Slightly diminishing returns but still functional.

jokes.text: Let me make a... cream pie... for you, okay? Then you can try it. See what you think.
jokes.setup: Charlie trying to get Mac and Dennis to let him join their cream pie business
jokes.punchline: Charlie offering to make a cream pie for Mac and Dennis so they can 'try it' — again, working as both a business pitch and something that sounds sexually provocative
jokes.explanation: The strategic pause before 'cream pie' makes this line work. Charlie's earnest offer reads more and more indecent with each additional beat in this extended sequence. Mid-tier in the extended misdirection chain.

jokes.text: Is Dee in on it? / Ew! God, no! Come on. Why would we... That's why she's at the factory, to distract her.
jokes.setup: Charlie asks if Dee is involved in the cream pie venture
jokes.punchline: Dennis's disgusted 'Ew! God, no!' — combined with the reveal that Dee was sent to the factory specifically to keep her away — is both a character beat and a continuation of the innuendo
jokes.explanation: Dennis's visceral disgust at the idea of Dee's involvement (in what appears to be a sex act) is consistent with his contempt for her. The reveal that the entire factory mission was a pretext to exclude Dee is a good structural payoff.

jokes.text: I do not want to taste your cream pie. / They taste great, I can guarantee it. / You've tasted yours? / Of course I have. Haven't you? / No! / I've tasted mine. I didn't like it. / I've tasted mine, yeah. I-I liked mine.
jokes.setup: Charlie insists his cream pies taste great; Mac and Dennis discuss whether they've tasted their own
jokes.punchline: Dennis: 'I've tasted mine. I didn't like it.' Mac: 'I've tasted mine, yeah. I liked mine.' — The confessional quality of these statements and their divergent verdicts is the peak of the misdirection sequence
jokes.explanation: This is the apex of the cream pie misdirection sequence and one of the episode's best moments. The structure is impeccable: Mac's refusal, Charlie's guarantee, Mac's shocked question ('You've tasted yours?'), Charlie's total nonchalance ('Of course I have'), Mac's horrified 'No!', and then the pièce de résistance — Dennis and Mac each giving divergent reviews of their own. Dennis not liking his, Mac liking his — delivered as straight self-assessment. The characterization is spot-on (Dennis being self-critical in a weird way, Mac being satisfied with himself), the economy is excellent, and the double-meaning operates at peak efficiency. Earned, not cheap.

jokes.text: Ew, dude! Little kids? / I'd love watching a kid do it. / Dude, you are gonna get in a lot of trouble.
jokes.setup: Charlie has just said little kids especially love cream pies
jokes.punchline: Charlie doubles down: 'I'd love watching a kid do it' — in his mind (eating a cream pie) but lands as the most damning possible statement in the sexual context
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's highest-impact moments. Charlie's completely innocent 'I'd love watching a kid do it' is delivered with no awareness of how it sounds. Mac's horrified 'Dude, you are gonna get in a lot of trouble' is the perfect straight-man response. The joke works because Charlie's obliviousness is total and consistent. Significantly darker than the earlier beats in the sequence, which is good escalation.

jokes.text: We're gonna sell them to everyone in Philly. Who the hell's gonna buy 'em? / Everyone's gonna buy 'em. Everyone loves them, especially little kids. / Ew, dude! Little kids? / I'd love watching a kid do it.
jokes.setup: Charlie is describing the cream pie business plan — selling to everyone in Philadelphia
jokes.punchline: Charlie's enthusiasm for 'little kids' enjoying cream pies triggers Mac's horror, and then Charlie saying 'I'd love watching a kid do it' escalates the double-entendre to its darkest and most absurd peak
jokes.explanation: The escalation into 'especially little kids' is a great dark subversion beat — Charlie means kids eating cream pies (dessert), which is completely innocent, but it sounds horrifying in context. 'I'd love watching a kid do it' is the dark apex. The show uses this technique brilliantly — Charlie is innocent, the joke is on the audience for where their minds go.

jokes.text: It's not like I'm gonna do it without the parents' permission. / No parent is gonna let you... / The parents are gonna watch. / They're not gonna watch! / We gotta go overseas for that.
jokes.setup: Mac is horrified by Charlie's cream pie plans involving children; Charlie explains the parents will be involved
jokes.punchline: Mac concedes 'we gotta go overseas for that' — implying this is so depraved even domestically it's impossible — which then makes Charlie's innocent 'that's as American as it gets' even funnier
jokes.explanation: Mac's horror escalating to 'we gotta go overseas for that' is a great dark beat that deepens the misunderstanding gap. The more Mac resists, the more committed he sounds to the wrong interpretation. Well-structured escalation.

jokes.text: That's as American as it gets. / You gotta think about this as a business venture. / The three of us combining our ingredients, making, like, one gigantic, delicious cream pie, some little kid sucking it down, and he's paying us for the pleasure.
jokes.setup: Charlie pitching the cream pie business to Mac and Dennis as an American tradition
jokes.punchline: 'Combining our ingredients, making one gigantic cream pie, some little kid sucking it down, and he's paying us for the pleasure' — an entirely innocent description of a baking business that is maximally incriminating in the other reading
jokes.explanation: This is the climax of the cream pie misdirection sequence and arguably the best single piece of writing in the episode. The sentence is grammatically and semantically innocent — it describes a child eating a cream pie dessert — but every single word choice functions maximally in the double-meaning reading. 'Combining our ingredients,' 'gigantic,' 'sucking it down,' 'paying us for the pleasure' — it couldn't be more perfectly constructed if it tried to be dirty. The structure is a 9 because the sentence lands EXACTLY at the moment of peak tension, right before the reveal. Earned comedy through precise craft.

jokes.text: Hang on a second. / What kind of cream pie are you talking about?
jokes.setup: Mac has been horrified by Charlie's description of the cream pie business venture
jokes.punchline: Mac (and Dennis, arriving late) suddenly realize they may not share the same understanding of 'cream pie' — the dawning awareness that Charlie might just mean actual pie
jokes.explanation: The reveal beat. 'What kind of cream pie are you talking about?' is the audience surrogate question — Mac finally questions his assumption. The economy is excellent: one sentence that pivots the entire extended sequence. The pause before it ('Hang on a second') gives it perfect comedic timing. This is the structural release valve for 4+ minutes of sustained misdirection, and it lands cleanly.

jokes.text: ♪♪ Cream pies. Everyone loves them. Comedians, baseball players, even protesters. / Cream pies are a rich American tradition, and also delicious. / Mmm, my mouth's getting wet just watching her eat that cream pie. / Asians know electronics. And fish. But Americans know cream pies... / God bless cream pies, and God bless America. / ♪♪ And China too.
jokes.setup: Frank has made a fake commercial/promotional video for his cream pie business pitch to the Chinese factory
jokes.punchline: The 'commercial' is an earnest propaganda piece for literal cream pies (the dessert) featuring stock imagery — but Frank's narration ('my mouth's getting wet just watching her eat that cream pie') reads as aggressively inappropriate while being technically innocent
jokes.explanation: Frank's commercial is a great set piece. 'My mouth's getting wet just watching her eat that cream pie' operating in the sustained double-entendre context is perfectly timed. 'And China too' as the afterthought international addendum to 'God Bless America' is a funny button. The nationalist cream pie propaganda framing is absurd and very Frank-appropriate.

jokes.text: Asians know electronics. And fish. But Americans know cream pies... Except for them.
jokes.setup: The cream pie commercial is building its pitch
jokes.punchline: 'Except for them' — presumably cutting to Asians who don't know cream pies, or possibly the gang itself; the casual xenophobia of the commercial is part of the joke
jokes.explanation: The commercial's casual nationalism is a decent gag — the structure of 'Asians know X, Americans know Y' mirrors the episode's xenophobia-as-character-flaw theme. 'Except for them' is a bit underdeveloped without visuals. Moderate.

jokes.text: Look, I'm an experienced businessman with a long history in Asian countries. Imagine my cream pie taste and know-how combined with your underpaid labor force? We could corner the cream pie market.
jokes.setup: Frank is pitching his cream pie business to the Chinese factory owner
jokes.punchline: Frank's pitch openly acknowledges 'your underpaid labor force' as a selling point — casual exploitation delivered as a straight business observation — while maintaining the cream pie double-entendre
jokes.explanation: Frank casually including 'underpaid labor force' as an asset in his pitch is perfect Frank character work — his amorality in business contexts is a consistent and always-fresh character note. The 'cream pie taste and know-how' maintains the ongoing double-meaning beautifully.

jokes.text: What do you mean, it's not the same kind of cream pie? / Oh, wait. I'll look.
jokes.setup: Frank's business partner (Charlie, via phone) apparently informs him that Mac and Dennis's 'cream pie' research is NOT the dessert kind
jokes.punchline: Frank suddenly learns the actual meaning of 'Asian cream pies' in the context of internet searches — his 'Oh wait, I'll look' implying he's about to verify this on a device, cutting to his horrified reaction
jokes.explanation: The reveal of what Mac and Dennis were actually researching, delivered to Frank mid-pitch, is a great structural moment. 'Oh wait, I'll look' cutting to 'Holy shit' is a clean comedic cut. The payoff of the entire misdirection sequence.

jokes.text: Holy shit. / Holy shi...
jokes.setup: Frank has looked up what 'cream pie' means in internet/pornographic context
jokes.punchline: His stunned double-take reaction — 'Holy shit. Holy shi...' cutting off mid-word — implies what he's seeing is simultaneously shocking and perhaps engaging
jokes.explanation: The cut-off 'Holy shi...' suggests Frank has become distracted mid-shock, possibly looking longer than necessary. The ellipsis doing a lot of heavy lifting. Frank's reaction implying potential interest in what he's seeing is a good dark character note.

jokes.text: Well, it looks like relying on old Dee really paid off for you guys after all, huh? / What are you talking about? / My series of accidents shut the whole factory down for, like, a couple days.
jokes.setup: Dee returns triumphant, believing she accomplished the mission
jokes.punchline: What she did was accidentally shut down the fish factory through her incompetence — which had the unintended effect of... causing a fish shortage, not espionage success
jokes.explanation: Dee's self-congratulation for a series of accidents is well-characterized. The irony that her bumbling accomplished something (factory shutdown) but it's the WRONG thing (fish shortage, not espionage) is a tidy payoff.

jokes.text: That's what's been driving up the price of fish. Snapper's way up. Snapper's through the roof. / Snapper's through the roof. / We're out of snapper, Dee! I told you. You can't count on her.
jokes.setup: Dee reveals her factory accidents shut everything down; Mac and Dennis realize this is why Guigino's had no snapper
jokes.punchline: The snapper price crisis — a running gag through the entire episode's restaurant scenes — is revealed to be Dee's fault; the final 'We're out of snapper, Dee! I told you. You can't count on her' ties the entire subplot together
jokes.explanation: Excellent callback structure — the entire snapper subplot (the $44 price, the waiter being out of fish, the multiple restaurant visits) is revealed to have been caused by Dee's incompetence. 'We're out of snapper, Dee!' as the final verdict on her mission is a satisfying structural payoff. The show doing tight plotting within apparent chaos is Always Sunny at its structural best.

jokes.text: We stole our Wi-Fi from that place too. Did you know that? Now we got no Wi-Fi because of you.
jokes.setup: Dee's factory shutdown is causing cascading problems; Mac and Dennis discover they were pirating Wi-Fi from the factory
jokes.punchline: Mac and Dennis were pirating internet from the factory they were 'spying' on — and Dee's shutdown cut off their connection (which was needed for their porn research)
jokes.explanation: A great structural reveal: Mac and Dennis lost their internet earlier in the episode because Dee shut down the factory from which they were stealing Wi-Fi. The layers here are perfect — they were 'spying' on the factory while completely dependent on it for their own activities. Dark and structurally tight.

jokes.text: Actually, we're pretty dependent on that Chinese factory. We need the Chinese, Dee. We need the...
jokes.setup: Mac and Dennis were worried the Chinese factory was spying on them and threatened Paddy's
jokes.punchline: Mac trails off mid-sentence realizing the irony — they need the Chinese factory for Wi-Fi and fish supply, completely reversing their paranoid opening stance
jokes.explanation: A satisfying thematic callback to the episode's opening premise. The gang's paranoia about the Chinese factory 'taking them over' is completely inverted — they're utterly dependent on it. The trailing '...for the cream, for the cr...' suggests Mac almost lets the porn slip, adding another layer. Good structural irony.

jokes.text: Listen, guys, uh, first of all, I'm gonna suggest that we reset our browser each time we do a research session. / That's a good idea. For privacy. / Right. Yeah, no more spying on ourselves.
jokes.setup: The spy operation post-mortem; Charlie dispenses lessons learned
jokes.punchline: Mac summarizes the spy operation's key failure: 'no more spying on ourselves' — the gang's spy operation was primarily spying on itself, and they're treating this as a productivity note
jokes.explanation: 'No more spying on ourselves' as a business takeaway from the episode's events is a great self-aware line. The gang treating self-surveillance as an inefficiency rather than a fundamental conceptual failure is perfect character comedy. Good economy.

jokes.text: Listen, guys, uh, first of all, I'm gonna suggest that we reset our browser each time we do a research session. / That's a good idea. For privacy. / Right. Yeah, no more spying on ourselves. / It's just all porn. Right.
jokes.setup: The gang wrapping up their spy operation and reviewing lessons learned
jokes.punchline: Charlie suggests resetting the browser 'for privacy,' which Mac calls a 'good idea' — the gang's spy operation lesson is to hide their porn browsing from each other, confirmed with 'it's just all porn'
jokes.explanation: A clean, efficient wrap to the episode's main mystery. The lesson from the spy operation is 'clear your browser history so no one finds your porn' — reduced to its absolute essential. 'No more spying on ourselves' as a takeaway from a spy episode is a good meta-beat. 'It's just all porn' as the final verdict on everyone's research is satisfyingly bleak.

jokes.text: Is it? Ah, we're all doing it. / I think what you're gonna find when you're spying on the general population is that everyone is just, uh, masturbating constantly.
jokes.setup: Frank reveals the Chinese factory's search history is also all porn; Dennis draws a universal conclusion
jokes.punchline: Dennis's grand sociological insight from the espionage operation is that the general population is 'just masturbating constantly' — a thesis delivered with the gravity of a think-tank finding
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best closing jokes. Dennis's confident, authoritative delivery of 'everyone is just masturbating constantly' as a research conclusion is an excellent button for an episode about spying. The escalation from 'it's all porn' to a universal sociological claim is perfectly calibrated. The clinical framing ('when you're spying on the general population') gives it a fake-academic weight that makes it funnier. Highly quotable.

jokes.text: We should keep spying on the Chinese though. / Oh, absolutely. / When I was over there, I looked at their search history... It's all porn too. / Is it? Ah, we're all doing it.
jokes.setup: Gang deciding whether to continue spying operations
jokes.punchline: Dee reports the Chinese factory's search history is also all porn — leading to Mac's resigned 'we're all doing it' as a universal human truth uncovered by their paranoid spy operation
jokes.explanation: 'We're all doing it' as the culminating insight of a spy operation is a great dark-humanist punchline. The gang's geopolitical paranoia resolves into 'everyone masturbates' — a classic Always Sunny deflation of pomposity. Good economy and a solid episode button.

jokes.text: I think what you're gonna find when you're spying on the general population is that everyone is just, uh, masturbating constantly. / I know I am. Yeah. / And yet you've never heard of a cream pie.
jokes.setup: Charlie delivers the episode's thesis statement about spying and human behavior; Mac confirms he masturbates constantly
jokes.punchline: Dennis's final line: 'And yet you've never heard of a cream pie' — calling back the entire misdirection sequence by pointing out that Mac, who masturbates constantly, somehow didn't know the sexual meaning of 'cream pie'
jokes.explanation: The episode's best closing line and one of its top jokes overall. The structure is perfect: Charlie establishes the thesis (everyone masturbates constantly), Mac self-confirms, and Dennis delivers the devastating callback — Mac, who apparently masturbates constantly, panicked about 'cream pies' because he'd never encountered the term. The economy is exceptional (nine words to close a 20-minute misdirection plot), the character integration is perfect (Dennis as the knowing sophisticate who finds Mac's innocence absurd), and it earns its shock through craft rather than just transgression. This is the kind of button line that makes an episode rewatchable.

tmdb_overview: Dennis and Mac enlist Dee to spy on the fish factory across the street, Charlie and Frank grow suspicious and decide to do some spying of their own.
